model.label: Segmented system: employment-based social insurance institutes for formal workers, tax-funded public services for everyone else (now largely run by IMSS-Bienestar), and a large out-of-pocket private sector

overview.statement: Mexico's constitution has recognised health as a fundamental right since reforms in 1983; the authors of a 2025 study judge that universal health coverage has not been achieved, and that fragmentation among public providers and limited public investment have held back progress toward equitable access.

The 2020 Observatory review describes three parallel parts: social insurance tied to employment, public services for people without social insurance backed by a financial protection scheme, and a private sector of providers, insurers and suppliers.

Formal-sector workers and their families are covered by separate social security institutions: ISSSTE for state workers (13.7 million people), the IMSS for private-sector employees (68.7 million), and smaller institutes for employees of the state oil company Pemex and the armed forces.

IMSS-Bienestar, a programme created in 1973 for marginalised populations, was expanded in 2022 to serve informal workers and the unemployed in place of INSABI, and by 2024 served 50 million people in the 23 of 32 states that signed federalisation agreements; in the states that opted out, the Ministry of Health and state health services serve 15.6 million people.
In 2018, 13.6% of the population (about 17.8 million people) had no public financial protection entitling them to free public care, and likely no private insurance either.
Legal eligibility for health coverage depends on a person's employment status, and differs according to whether the job is public or private and formal or informal.

financing.statement: The IMSS is financed jointly by workers, employers and the federal government: worker and employer contributions go straight to the IMSS, while the government pays its share through the federal budget.

Seguro Popular, started in 2003, copied the three-way funding of social insurance: the federal government paid a fixed fee per enrolled person (largely from rising oil revenue), states added half that amount, and enrollees above the poverty level were to pay an annual income-related fee.

The 2020 review reports that public services for people without social insurance, run by the federal and state governments, are paid for mainly from general taxes and other government revenue, and to a smaller extent from user fees paid out of pocket.
The 2020 review cites estimates that 7.8% of Mexicans had private health insurance, mostly policies covering major medical expenses.

Under the Social Security Law, the cash benefits of IMSS sickness and maternity insurance are funded by a contribution of 1% of the worker's contribution wage base, split 70% employer, 25% worker and 5% federal government.

To fund medical care in kind for IMSS pensioners and their dependants, the Social Security Law sets a contribution of 1.5% of the contribution wage base: 1.05% paid by the employer, 0.375% by the worker and 0.075% by the State.

ISSSTE health insurance for federal government employees is funded by worker contributions of 2.75% of basic salary (for active workers and their families) plus 0.625% (for pensioners), employer contributions from government agencies of 7.375% plus 0.72%, and a daily per-worker social contribution from the federal government.

Under the General Health Law, the federal government funds free health services, medicines and supplies each year through IMSS-BIENESTAR, as set in the federal budget; the amount may not fall below the previous year's, subject to budget availability. Where IMSS-BIENESTAR does not provide this care, the money goes to the states.

State governments also contribute to free care for people without social security, in amounts set by coordination agreements, and their contributions must rise in the same proportion as the federal funding.

Each year IMSS-BIENESTAR must channel the equivalent of 11% of the combined federal and state funding for free care into the Health for Wellbeing Fund (Fondo de Salud para el Bienestar), whose technical committee approves its use.

In their annual income tax return, individuals may deduct fees for medical, dental, psychology and nutrition services and hospital costs paid for themselves, a spouse or partner, or parents and children, provided payment is made electronically, by cheque or by card.

Individuals may also deduct premiums for private medical insurance that complements or is independent of public social security health services, when the insured person is the taxpayer, a spouse or partner, or a direct ascendant or descendant.

With one listed exception, an individual's total personal deductions are capped at the lower of five times the annual value of the UMA (Mexico's reference unit for fees and limits) or 15% of total income, including tax-exempt income.
Employers may deduct, as a business expense, the premiums they pay for medical insurance for their workers.

Workers whose pay plus tax-exempt welfare benefits exceeds seven times the annual minimum wage normally have that exemption limited, but the limit does not apply to medical insurance or to reimbursed medical, dental and hospital costs granted generally under laws or employment contracts, provided the employer-side deduction requirements are met.

Using Finance Ministry estimates, CIEP puts the revenue forgone in 2026 through personal income tax deductions, chiefly for medical, dental, psychology, nutrition and hospital costs, at 0.0337% of GDP, close to its historical average of 0.0321%.

CIEP calculates that the 2026 budget proposal of September 2025 would raise public health spending by 5.9% in real terms over 2025 but leave it 4.7% below what was spent in 2024, at 2.6% of GDP (MXN 996,528 million), under half of the 6% of GDP the WHO suggests.

In the 2026 budget proposal, most of the increase went to the IMSS (an extra MXN 58,213.9 million), while the Ministry of Health faced a cut of MXN 2,228.6 million and IMSS-Bienestar a real increase of 0.8%, although CIEP notes it serves the largest number of people.

IMSS's sickness and maternity insurance ran a deficit in every year from 2020 to 2025: its revenue grew by an average 3.5% a year in real terms against 4.2% for spending, the operating deficit equalled 23% of revenue, and the 2025 deficit was 40.3% larger than in 2020.

As of December 2025, medical care in kind under IMSS sickness and maternity insurance was funded by a fixed contribution equal to 20.40% of the UMA from the employer and 14.83% of the UMA from the federal government (35.23% in total), plus, on the contribution wage above three times the UMA, 1.10% from the employer and 0.40% from the worker.

financing.statement: The 14.83%-of-UMA contribution is a daily payment for each insured person set by the Social Security Law and updated every quarter; in December 2025 it was 16.78 pesos.
The Social Security Law makes the federal government pay IMSS a daily amount for every insured person toward medical care in kind, updated each quarter in line with the national consumer price index.

covered.statement: Until its abolition, Seguro Popular promised enrollees a benefit package free at the point of use; its core catalogue (CAUSES) listed 294 interventions across prevention, general and specialist medicine, emergencies, general surgery and obstetrics.

Under Seguro Popular, the package was revised every two years, and high-cost treatments for its catastrophic expenditure fund were chosen through a General Health Council consultation using criteria such as cost-effectiveness and affordability, with a technical committee deciding what to fund depending on the money available; the fund covered 66 high-cost interventions.

Medicines and devices must be registered by the General Health Council before each public institution decides whether to put them on its own approved list, based on whether it considers them necessary and affordable.

Seguro Popular paid for a defined essential package that included tertiary care and medicines, funded according to enrolment; INSABI in practice covered less, excluded tertiary care, and did not clearly define how it was financed.
Emergency departments in both public and private hospitals take patients regardless of which institution covers them.
As of the 2020 review, long-term care was practically non-existent, palliative care policy was recent, and mental health services were underdeveloped and centred on psychiatric hospitals.
INSABI took over from Seguro Popular on 1 January 2020 with the aim of providing health services, medicines and supplies free of charge at all levels of care to people without social security.

cost_sharing.statement: Each of the public contributory schemes (IMSS, ISSSTE and other social insurance institutions, and formerly the Seguro Popular system) officially covers its own population and provides most services without user fees.
Seguro Popular was free for members in the lower five income deciles, which include most Mexicans, while higher-income members owed an annual contribution tied to income.
In practice most Seguro Popular members in the higher income deciles were enrolled without the contribution being collected.
People without Seguro Popular (later INSABI) cover, and even people with other insurance, can use Ministry of Health hospitals and state facilities by paying out of pocket on an income-related scale.
Medicines made up the largest share of out-of-pocket health spending among households covered by Seguro Popular/INSABI (64.5%) and mixed-insurance households (63.6%).

The 2020 review found that long waits, lack of trust and missing medicines push many people to private providers, and that the probability of paying out of pocket is high even for people who have public insurance.

According to the national household income and expenditure survey, average monthly current monetary spending on health per household was 535 pesos in 2024 (in 2024 pesos), up from 382 pesos in 2016: an 8.0% rise since 2022 and a 40.0% rise over 2016-2024.

financial_hardship.statement: Financial protection improved for most households between 2000 and 2014, especially among Seguro Popular members, but deteriorated after 2020 once INSABI had replaced Seguro Popular, with catastrophic and excessive health spending reaching their highest levels among mixed-insurance households by 2022.

Households with social security consistently bore the lowest financial burden from health costs, while uninsured and INSABI-affiliated households were at substantially higher risk; growing use of private care, especially for medicines, added to out-of-pocket spending.

Between 2018 and 2020 the share of households without health insurance almost doubled, from 8.8% (3 million households) to 16.5% (5.8 million); the study found large increases in households with catastrophic spending (estimated 18.4%, 95% CI 6.1-30.7), and significant increases in catastrophic, impoverishing and excessive spending only among uninsured households.

The authors conclude that ending Seguro Popular and replacing it with INSABI early in the COVID-19 pandemic reduced health coverage, and that this and the pandemic together raised out-of-pocket spending and catastrophic and excessive spending in 2018-2020, most of all for uninsured households and those in central and southern states.

additional_care.statement: Private health insurance covered nearly 8% of the population, many of them higher-income people who also have IMSS or ISSSTE cover and get private insurance as an employment benefit; most private care is paid out of pocket on a fee-for-service basis.

A 2025 commentary reports that visits to retail pharmacy clinics typically cost US$2-5, with some services free, and that the clinics receive hundreds of millions of visits a year, which the authors read as a sign of both high demand and deep unmet need in the public sector.
Private hospitals held 24.3% of hospital beds and accounted for 25.1% of hospital discharges.
The private sector's share of outpatient care grew from 38% in 2006 to 66% in 2022, even though two national programmes sought to extend public coverage to nearly 50 million people.
Private use is common even among the publicly insured: 30.9% of IMSS members, 28.4% of ISSSTE members and 31.1% of members of the now-dismantled Seguro Popular had sought care in the private sector.
About 25% of hospital admissions in the study's data were in private facilities, peaking at 34% in 2021, which the authors link to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The same commentary says doctors in these clinics often face pressure to prescribe in order to meet sales quotas, and cites population studies suggesting their patients are prescribed more active substances per visit than patients of public or private institutions.

A 2026 commentary reports that retail pharmacy clinics began expanding in 2010, when a regulation required a medical prescription for antibiotics sold in pharmacies; they grew fastest in 2010-2013, from 2 to 4 per 100,000 people, and reached 8 per 100,000 in 2023.

access.statement: Up to 71% of general physicians work in the public sector, and physician density varies by state from 0.6 per 1,000 people in the State of Mexico to 1.8 per 1,000 in Mexico City.
High-cost equipment is scarce: Mexico had 2.6 MRI machines per million people, against 6.8 in Brazil and an OECD average of 15.6.
Hospitals are concentrated in cities: only 46 hospitals (3.3%) were in rural localities.
Because of long waits for consultations and specialist care and shortcomings in quality, people tend to seek private care or even pay out of pocket for Ministry of Health services.
A 2026 study cites Mexican evidence that long waits, staff shortages and frequent medicine stock-outs in public facilities push insured households to pay for private consultations.

Of 1,891 municipalities studied, 1,187 (62.8%) had no hospital beds; these 'healthcare deserts' had 42.5% higher avoidable mortality before the pandemic (2015-2019), with an incidence rate ratio of 1.353 after adjusting for age structure.

A 2026 evaluation using the 2024 national health and nutrition survey compared uninsured people in states that joined IMSS-BIENESTAR with those in states that kept their own health services: people in IMSS-BIENESTAR states more often reported a health need, but in both groups a low share was treated in the public sector, and the chance of receiving care did not differ between the two kinds of state.

In Mexico's official poverty measurement, the threshold for lacking access to health services is having no affiliation with, or entitlement to medical services from, a public institution or private provider.

locator.section: Carencia por acceso a los servicios de salud, p. 19

access.statement: In 2024, 34.2% of the population (44.5 million people) lacked access to health services by this measure; the share had risen from 15.6% in 2016 to 39.1% in 2022, then fell by 4.9 percentage points between 2022 and 2024, meaning 5.9 million more people reported being affiliated with or entitled to care from a public or private institution.

locator.section: Carencia por acceso a los servicios de salud, p. 20, gráfica 13

access.statement: In 2024 the lack of access to health services by this measure affected 30.1% of the urban population (30.6 million people) and 48.7% of the rural population (13.9 million).

locator.section: Carencia por acceso a los servicios de salud, p. 20-21, cuadro 4

outcomes.statement: Heart disease, diabetes and malignant tumours were the three leading causes of death nationally in 2024, for women and for men.
The 2020 review reports that Mexico has the second-highest overall obesity prevalence in the world, after the United States, and the highest share of overweight and obese children.
Maternal mortality fell from 59.3 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2000 to 47.3 in 2018, then rose from 48.7 in 2019 to 72.4 in 2022.

Among people without social security, preventable and treatable mortality increased after 2012 (by 3.26% and 5.54% a year respectively after 2018), while both declined steadily among people with social security.

Citing a World Bank report, the 2025 study notes age-standardised rates of 435 preventable and 257 treatable deaths per 100,000 in Mexico, above those of Peru, Brazil, Colombia, Chile and Costa Rica, where avoidable mortality has been falling.
Of 4,960,244 deaths under age 75 in the study, 81.2% were classed as avoidable.

Coverage of BCG, hepatitis B, pentavalent and MMR vaccination peaked in 2006-2012 under Seguro Popular and fell to 31% in 2021 under INSABI; the brief links the drop to weak primary care, lower demand, vaccine shortfalls, lower spending and poor stewardship.

In the GBD 2016 Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index, Mexico was in the sixth of ten deciles nationally; six Mexican states reached the seventh decile, most were in the sixth, and four states, all on the southern border, were in the fifth.
Mexico's HAQ Index improved much faster in 1990-2000 than in 2000-2016, while absolute inequalities narrowed somewhat by 2016, from a 20.9-point to a 17.0-point difference.
Mexico's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 52.5 (95% uncertainty interval 48.7-56.8) in 2019 in the GBD 2019 study, 17.3 points higher than in 1990.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location, 2019 overall (0-74 years) and absolute change 1990-2019 overall

costs.statement: The public share of total health spending rose from 43.7% in 2000 to 53.8% in 2015, partly because of Seguro Popular, which helped cut the out-of-pocket share from 53.9% to 41.3%; out-of-pocket spending nonetheless stayed far above the OECD average of 19%.
Public health spending rose from 2000 to 2012, faster for people without social security, then levelled off for both groups in 2012-2018.
Public spending as a share of total health spending fell from 55% in 2020 to 51% in 2021, a level last seen in 2009, and was still below its earlier peak of 55% in 2024 despite a slight rise.
The 2025 study puts Mexico's public health spending at 3.2% of GDP, low next to Argentina (over 5%) and Costa Rica and Colombia (over 4%).

what_works.statement: The 2020 review credits Seguro Popular, and possibly generic medicines and low-cost private consultations, with substantial reductions in catastrophic health spending, though out-of-pocket spending fell only slightly.
Early evaluations of Seguro Popular found more use of hospital services, wider access to primary care and more births in public hospitals.

The rollout of Seguro Popular's financing system reduced geographic disparities in access for people without social security by expanding hospitals and primary care clinics, and demand grew most in the most marginalised municipalities.

While Seguro Popular was expanding, private use of outpatient care fell from 38% in 2006 to 31% in 2012, before rising to 43% in 2018; over 2006-2018 Seguro Popular's coverage grew from 14% to 37% of the population.
Under Seguro Popular the list of covered benefits was regularly updated and published, and compliance with it was checked continuously at patient and facility level.

problems.statement: The 2020 review calls the system's segmented governance perhaps the biggest obstacle to a universal system, because the social insurance institutions largely operate outside Ministry of Health regulation, which hinders a stronger regulator able to tackle access and quality problems.

The 2025 study argues that creating parallel schemes for informal workers has institutionalised lower health entitlements for people without social security, reinforcing their exclusion from comprehensive care and social benefits.

The 2025 study notes that a single national system on the English or French model could in principle achieve universal coverage, but that those countries have far less informal employment (6.5% in the UK and 3.1% in France) than Mexico, where informality affects 55.5% of the labour force.

Comparing Seguro Popular's last two years with INSABI's first two, the authors report steep falls in specialised care between 2018 and 2021: heart-attack care dropped 80.7%, neonatal intensive care 78.4%, childhood cancer care 74.5%, and breast, cervical and prostate cancer care 50.1%, 48.2% and 41% respectively.
A 2026 study cites evidence that INSABI's rollout brought confusion over entitlements, limited operating capacity and disrupted services, including access to medicines.
The authors argue that dismantling Seguro Popular while trying to set up a new programme in 2020-21 left the health system more vulnerable during the worst period of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The 2020 review describes the IMSS as technically bankrupt because of unfunded entitlements, projecting that by 2030 up to 63% of its income could be absorbed by the pension fund.

The 2020 review judges that the goal of a universal national health system fell short under the 2012-2018 administration: per capita public health spending fell for the first time in decades because of small but significant cuts to funding for the uninsured, and Seguro Popular did not add significant new high-cost treatments.

A systematic review found that studies described the lack of an explicit national policy and gaps in regulation and transparency, and reported problems with the supply, selection, purchasing and distribution of medicines and with spending on them.

The Seguro Popular commission had to report each year to Congress on its finances and coverage; the 2020 review notes that when INSABI replaced Seguro Popular these accountability mechanisms were abolished and nothing replaced them.

From 2000 to 2018 seven in ten maternal deaths were among women without social security, falling to six in ten from 2020; these deaths were more common among younger, less-schooled, unmarried and rural women and in areas with more Indigenous people and greater marginalisation.

Avoidable mortality was strongly clustered in southern Mexico, and by 2024 the gap in avoidable mortality between 'healthcare desert' municipalities and adequately supplied ones had widened about fivefold, from about 12 to 69 per 100,000 people.

The authors of a 2026 review write that austerity under the previous administration, together with long-standing weaknesses in how medicines were procured, led to supply disruptions, public discontent and protests.

A 2022 policy report argues that the health system changes made by the 2018-2024 government caused major setbacks in guaranteeing access to medicines, with effects, in the authors' view, on user and citizen satisfaction, household health spending and health conditions.

reforms.statement: A 2026 article frames the IMSS-Bienestar model around primary care and integrated service networks, and argues that its challenges are organisational, political and institutional: rebuilding state capacity, redefining coordination, and aligning financing, service provision and territorial responsibility for health.

According to the authors, INSABI's poor performance led the López Obrador government to end it in 2023 and set up IMSS-Bienestar under the Mexican Social Security Institute, which now provides care directly to the uninsured.

In 2018-2024 the government dismantled Seguro Popular's financing system, centralised the purchasing of medicines and supplies, recentralised state health services, and created INSABI and later IMSS-Bienestar for people without social security; the aim was to unify care under the IMSS, but only 23 states signed federalisation agreements, leaving nine with their own services.

Unlike Seguro Popular, which acted as a public insurer reimbursing providers (including some private hospitals), INSABI provided care directly through public facilities and, for catastrophic illnesses, supplied medicines and equipment to public specialty hospitals.
Seguro Popular closed in January 2020, and Mexico began a complex, wide-ranging reorganisation of its health system.

INSABI was created in 2019 to replace Seguro Popular, which had run from 2003 to 2019; its critics argued Seguro Popular had fostered corruption and 'neoliberal' practices, and INSABI assumed that removing these would free enough money for universal coverage.

Key reforms toward the constitutional right to health were the 2003 creation of the Seguro Popular financing system, run jointly by federal and state governments; the 2006 Strategy for Portability and Convergence, to coordinate high-specialty hospital care across social insurance and Ministry of Health services regardless of affiliation; and a 2014 reform to make the Seguro Popular financing system more accountable.

The decree creating the Servicio Universal de Salud (SUS, Universal Health Service) sets it up as a compulsory mechanism to coordinate and operationally integrate the federal public institutions that provide health care, plus any state health services that join, aiming at progressive, effective and non-discriminatory access for everyone, subject to the level of care needed and each institution's installed, financial and budget capacity.

The SUS has a national register, administered by the Ministry of Health, that is built as people sign up for a health credential; registration is free and uses the CURP population registry code as the unique identifier, and the credential is meant to ease access to the network's services.

On 7 April 2026 the President announced the decree creating the Universal Health Service, stating that its aim is for people to be able to use any of the three public systems (IMSS, IMSS-Bienestar and ISSSTE); registration for the credential was to run from 13 to 30 April at 2,059 Welfare Ministry offices, starting with people aged 85 and over.

According to the government's announced timetable, exchange of specialised services between institutions is to begin in the second half of 2027, and in 2028 the plan is to add universal filling of prescriptions, specialist outpatient consultations, referred hospital admissions and open access to primary care for chronic conditions.
A 2026 review notes that the ongoing changes it describes have been maintained under President Claudia Sheinbaum (2024-2030), the first woman to hold the office in Mexico.

On 31 October 2024 the Minister of Health presented a new consolidated purchasing model for medicines and medical supplies for 2025-2026, in which 26 institutions would take part and which would be open to national and international suppliers; officials described it as the largest such purchase in the country's history by volume and number of items.

As the ministry described the mechanism, the Ministry of Health diagnoses, plans and supervises the purchase, each institution sets its needs by item and delivery point, the state-owned company Birmex carries out the purchase, and the institutions sign contracts and receive the goods; the purchase was to cover 4,454 items of medicines and supplies with a budget of 130 billion pesos.

Under the decree, the SUS is a network built on capacity shared between IMSS, ISSSTE, IMSS-BIENESTAR, PEMEX hospitals and clinics, the federal reference hospitals and the National Institutes of Health, and open to other public providers that choose to join, such as state health services outside IMSS-BIENESTAR; through it, free medical care and medicines are to be provided under rules to be issued.
The SUS network is to work by institutions exchanging services with budgetary and financial compensation: the institution a patient belongs to must reimburse the institution that treats them.

The decree phases in the exchange of services between institutions; the first stage, from 1 January 2027, prioritises free emergency care in any facility until discharge, care for high-risk pregnancies including obstetric emergencies, and heart-attack and stroke protocols with access to any facility and transfer to better-equipped units.

The priorities listed in the decree also include keeping outpatient treatment going, at the institution where it began, for patients with chronic kidney failure, cancer, transplants, HIV or haemophilia who lose social-security entitlement; completing vaccinations at any public unit; and primary care consultations, including prescriptions, at the unit nearest the patient.
A second stage of the exchange of services, from 1 July 2027, is to add laboratory and imaging tests (including CT, ultrasound and MRI) and radiotherapy sessions.

changelog.note: Profile created: 78 claims from 11 sources anchored to fingerprinted passages and support-reviewed; 30 statements corrected after an independent support review and 2 re-anchored.

Backfill: 22 claims added from the 2026 Servicio Universal de Salud decree and presidential announcement, the Ministry of Health's 2025-2026 consolidated medicines purchase, INEGI's 2024 poverty-measurement and ENIGH 2024 releases, a 2026 IMSS-BIENESTAR evaluation, a 2026 review, a 2022 policy report and the GBD 2016 and 2019 HAQ Index studies; all support-reviewed (7 statements corrected, 2 re-anchored). OECD Health at a Glance 2025 could not be downloaded (403).

Data-age backfill: dropped 6 claims resting on 2003-2015 data (IMSS job turnover 2014, 2015 financing shares, private insurance share 2000-2015, spending for the uninsured 2003-2009, bed gap 2003-2006, spending growth 2001-2015); marked the 2000-2015 public/out-of-pocket share trend as historical; replaced 2015 causes of death with INEGI 2024 registered-death statistics; replaced the 2015 pharmacy-clinic count with two 2025-2026 Lancet Regional Health - Americas commentaries (3 claims). New claims support-reviewed (3 statements corrected, 1 re-anchored).
